label: Day 1
summary: The first day is mostly recovery and skin-to-skin.
development: {name} sees best about 8–12 inches away — face distance — and already knows your voice.
feeding: Colostrum only and in teaspoons. Three or more feeds today is typical; many newborns are sleepy after birth.
sleep: Long stretches of sleep are normal today. Wake {them} to feed at least every three hours.
heads_up: Expect at least one wet diaper and one black, tarry meconium stool.
facts: The vitamin K shot at birth prevents a rare bleeding disorder that is devastating when it happens. It is one dose, once. | Skin-to-skin steadies temperature, blood sugar and breathing, and brings the milk in sooner. | Back to sleep, on a firm flat surface, nothing else in the bed — from the very first nap.

label: Day 2
summary: Waking up — and often much hungrier.
development: Reflexes are on show: rooting, sucking, grasping and the startle reflex.
feeding: Cluster feeding often starts tonight. Aim for 8–12 feeds in 24 hours.
sleep: The second night is famously unsettled. Skin-to-skin and frequent feeds are the answer.
heads_up: Two wet diapers and at least one meconium stool today.
facts: The newborn screening heel prick is done at 24–48 hours, along with a hearing screen and a pulse-ox check for heart defects. | Cluster feeding tonight is how supply gets set, not a sign that anything is short. | Sign the birth certificate paperwork before discharge — it is far easier than doing it later.

label: Day 3
summary: Milk usually comes in around now.
development: {name} turns toward familiar voices and calms to being held.
feeding: Milk transitions from colostrum and breasts may feel full and firm. Keep feeding 8–12 times.
sleep: Still no rhythm — sleep follows feeds, day and night alike.
heads_up: Stools turn green-brown as they transition. Weight loss of up to about 7–10% is expected by now.
facts: Up to 7–10% weight loss by day three is expected. The checks are about the trend, not one number. | Engorgement peaks days 3–5: feed often, warmth just before a feed, cold after. | Ask for a lactation consultant while you are still in hospital, even if feeding seems fine.

label: Day 4
summary: Output climbs as feeding settles.
development: Hands stay fisted near the face and the head still needs full support.
feeding: Swallowing should be audible during a feed. Output climbs with intake.
sleep: Days and nights are still swapped for most babies.
heads_up: Four wet diapers and three stools. Jaundice often peaks on days 3–5 and your team will check for it.
facts: Jaundice peaks days 3–5. Yellow reaching the belly or below, or a baby too sleepy to feed, is a call today. | 400 IU of vitamin D a day is recommended for breastfed and partly breastfed babies, starting in the first days. | The cord stump falls off between one and three weeks. Keep it dry and fold the diaper below it.

label: Day 5
summary: Yellow, seedy stools mean feeding is working.
development: Eyes track a slowly moving face for a moment or two.
feeding: Feeds may shorten as {name} gets more efficient. Still 8–12 in 24 hours.
sleep: Short stretches, around the clock.
heads_up: Five wet diapers and three yellow stools. The cord stump is drying out.
facts: Yellow seedy stools mean milk is transferring — count diapers rather than minutes at the breast. | A fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher under three months is an immediate call, day or night. | Sleep when you can, in any stretch you can get. It is not a luxury at this point.

label: Days 6–7
summary: The first week closes and weight should start climbing back.
development: {name} calms to your smell and voice more reliably than to anything else.
feeding: Six or more wet and three or more stools a day is the reassuring pattern from here.
sleep: 14–17 hours a day in total in stretches of two to four hours.
heads_up: The first weight check is usually days 3–5 with a follow-up around day 10–14.
facts: The first pediatric visit is usually 3–5 days after discharge — weight, jaundice and feeding. | Newborns need waking to feed every three hours or so until weight gain is established. | Accept the offers of food and laundry. They are the ones that actually help.

label: Week 2
summary: Back to birth weight, and a first growth spurt.
development: Brief eye contact and slightly longer alert windows appear.
feeding: A growth spurt around days 7–10 means more frequent feeds for a day or two.
sleep: Still two to four hour stretches. A day-night difference has not arrived yet.
heads_up: Most babies are back to birth weight by day 10–14. The cord stump usually comes away this week.
facts: Most babies are back to birth weight by 10–14 days. | Start tummy time now — a few minutes several times a day, always awake and watched. It builds the neck strength everything else depends on. | Postpartum bleeding should be easing. Soaking a pad an hour, clots bigger than a golf ball, fever, or a bad headache are all same-day calls.

label: Week 3
summary: Fussier evenings are normal and they peak around week six.
development: {name} holds {their} head up briefly during tummy time.
feeding: Feeds settle into a rhythm and another spurt often lands around now.
sleep: One slightly longer night stretch may start to appear.
heads_up: Evening fussing often starts this week. Hold, walk, and share the load with someone.
facts: Evening fussiness climbs from about now and peaks near six weeks. It passes on its own. | Room-share without bed-sharing for at least six months — it is one of the largest single reductions in SIDS risk. | Ask anyone holding the baby whether they are up to date on whooping cough and flu.

label: Week 4
summary: One month in — more awake, more responsive.
development: Follows a face across the midline and quiets to a familiar voice.
feeding: 8–12 feeds a day or a bottle every two to three hours.
sleep: 15–16 hours a day, still spread right across the clock.
heads_up: The one-month check-up usually lands about now. Bring the log with you.
facts: Crying totals are climbing toward their peak. It is a stage in every baby, not a verdict on anything you are doing. | Handing the baby to someone else, or putting them down somewhere safe for five minutes, is good parenting. | The six-week postpartum check is for you — mood, bleeding, healing and contraception. Keep it.

label: Weeks 5–6
summary: The first real social smile.
development: A responsive smile usually appears at six to eight weeks — the first two-way conversation.
feeding: The six-week growth spurt is the biggest of the early months.
sleep: The longest night stretch often reaches four or five hours.
heads_up: Crying peaks around six weeks and eases from there. It is ok to put {them} down somewhere safe and step away for a few minutes when you need to.
facts: A responsive smile arrives at six to eight weeks and is worth marking down. | Crying peaks now, often two to three hours a day, and falls away through months three and four. | When it is too much: baby on their back in the crib, walk out, breathe, come back. Always the right call.

label: Weeks 7–8
summary: Cooing starts, and so does the two-month visit.
development: Vowel sounds and much stronger head control on the tummy.
feeding: Bottles are typically 4–5 oz six to eight times a day; nursing every two to three hours.
sleep: A clearer day-night pattern begins to form.
heads_up: Two-month check-up and the first large round of immunisations.
facts: The two-month visit brings the first main round of immunisations. | Fever medicine after shots is dosed by weight — get the number at the visit rather than guessing later. | Aim for 15–30 minutes of tummy time across the day by now, in short bursts.

label: Weeks 9–10
summary: Hands are discovered.
development: {name} finds {their} hands, swipes at toys and holds {their} head steady when upright.
feeding: Feeds are quicker and more efficient — a short feed is not always a small meal.
sleep: Night stretches of five or six hours are common but far from universal.
heads_up: Drooling and chewing on fists is exploring, not usually teething this early.
facts: Babies this age take turns in a 'conversation'. Pausing for a reply is what builds language. | Hands go in the mouth constantly now. It is exploration, not necessarily hunger.

label: Weeks 11–13
summary: Laughing out loud.
development: Belly laughs, purposeful reaching and pushing up onto the forearms.
feeding: Nursing sessions settle to 15–20 minutes and bottles to around 5 oz.
sleep: Total sleep drops to about 14–16 hours and naps organise into three or four a day.
heads_up: A sleep regression around three or four months is a developmental leap, not a step backwards.
facts: Colic, if it arrived, usually resolves by three to four months. | Rolling can start any time now. Never leave the baby alone on a bed, sofa or changing table. | Night stretches lengthen around now for many babies — genuinely, not just anecdotally.

label: 3 months
summary: Rolling front-to-back may arrive.
development: Rolls one way, bears weight on the legs when held, and studies {their} own hands.
feeding: Still milk only — solids come at around six months. Roughly 24–32 oz a day.
sleep: Two long naps plus a catnap. Some babies sleep through and plenty do not.
heads_up: Keep the sleep space flat, firm and empty. Rolling means never leaving {them} on a raised surface.
facts: Once rolling starts, swaddling has to stop. | Milk only is recommended to about six months; solids before four months are not advised. | Drool and fist-chewing at three months is usually salivary glands switching on, not teething.

label: 4 months
summary: Sitting with support and grabbing everything.
development: Grabs and mouths anything in reach and rolls both directions for some.
feeding: Milk only. Watch for readiness signs for solids: sitting up, head control, interest in food.
sleep: Naps consolidate and a bedtime routine starts to earn its keep.
heads_up: Four-month check-up and immunisations. Teething can start any time from now.
facts: The four-month visit brings the next immunisations and a developmental check. | The 'four-month regression' is a real shift to adult-like sleep cycles. It settles. | Introducing peanut and egg between four and six months lowers allergy risk. Ask at this visit about the right timing for your baby.

label: 5 months
summary: Sitting propped up, and very loud.
development: Squeals, blows raspberries and passes a toy from hand to hand.
feeding: Some families start solids at the end of this month on their doctor's advice.
sleep: Around 12–15 hours in total across the day with three naps.
heads_up: Everything goes in the mouth now. Check the floor for anything smaller than a toilet-roll tube.
facts: Readiness for solids is sitting with support, steady head control, and reaching for your food — not an age alone. | Rolling both ways and grabbing everything means hot drinks go nowhere near a lap.

label: 6 months
summary: First tastes.
development: Sits without support for short spells and responds to {their} own name.
feeding: Solids usually begin: iron-rich first foods alongside milk, which stays the main nutrition.
sleep: Three naps. Night wakings often return alongside new skills.
heads_up: Six-month check-up. Ask about introducing allergens — early and regular is the current advice.
facts: Iron stores laid down before birth run out around six months, which is why first foods should be iron-rich. | No honey before twelve months — infant botulism is rare and serious. | Teething often starts now. Something cold and firm to gnaw; no amber necklaces, no numbing gels.

label: 7 months
summary: On the move — or trying hard to be.
development: Rocks on hands and knees, gets into a sitting position, and transfers objects deliberately.
feeding: Two or three small solid meals a day and thicker textures.
sleep: About 11–14 hours including two or three naps.
heads_up: Time to lower the crib mattress and look at the room from floor height.
facts: Choking risks: no whole grapes, nuts, popcorn or hard raw vegetable chunks. | It takes eight to fifteen exposures for many babies to accept a new flavour. Keep offering without pressure. | Water in an open cup with meals is the right drink alongside milk.

label: 8 months
summary: Crawling, cruising and separation anxiety.
development: Pulls to stand, crawls, and understands no. Wariness of strangers peaks.
feeding: Three meals plus milk. Finger foods build the pincer grasp.
sleep: Separation anxiety can disturb nights for a few weeks.
heads_up: Baby-proof properly now: outlets, stairs, cords and furniture that can tip.
facts: Separation anxiety peaks between eight and ten months and is a sign of secure attachment. | Once they pull to stand, lower the crib mattress the same day. | Babyproof at floor level: outlet covers, cabinet latches, stair gates, blind cords tied up out of reach.

label: 9 months
summary: Pointing, waving and babbling with intent.
development: Says mama and dada without meaning them yet, waves, and plays peekaboo.
feeding: Three meals and two snacks. A cup can be introduced alongside.
sleep: Usually two naps, morning and afternoon.
heads_up: Nine-month check-up, usually with a developmental screening.
facts: The nine-month visit usually includes a developmental screening questionnaire. | Reading a few minutes every day is among the best-evidenced things for later language. | Responding to their babble as if it were speech teaches turn-taking faster than anything else.

label: 10 months
summary: Cruising the furniture.
development: Cruises sideways along furniture and stands alone for a second or two.
feeding: Self-feeding gets messy. The mess is the practice.
sleep: One nap may start dropping for some. Most keep two until well after a year.
heads_up: Shoes are not needed indoors — bare feet help balance.
facts: Pulling up and cruising means falls. Pad the sharp corners at head height rather than following them around. | Self-feeding is meant to be messy — the mess is the motor practice.

label: 11 months
summary: Almost one.
development: First deliberate words and following a simple instruction paired with a gesture.
feeding: Whole cow's milk usually starts at 12 months. Check the timing with your pediatrician.
sleep: 11–14 hours a day including naps.
heads_up: Plan the one-year visit. Bloodwork for iron and lead is common at it.
facts: Plan the move from bottle to open cup around twelve months; longer bottle use affects teeth and appetite. | The first dental visit is recommended by the first birthday.

label: 12–13 months
summary: First steps, and a much smaller appetite.
development: Walking usually starts between 9 and 18 months and every part of that range is normal.
feeding: Appetite drops sharply as growth slows. Offer, do not push.
sleep: Around 11–14 hours. Naps drop toward one by about 15 months.
heads_up: Twelve-month check-up and immunisations. Bottles give way to a cup gradually.
facts: Whole cow's milk can start at twelve months, about 16 oz a day. Past 24 oz it displaces iron-rich food. | Appetite drops sharply after one because growth slows. Offer, do not push. | Rear-facing in the car for as long as the seat allows — well past the first birthday.

label: 14–15 months
summary: Words arrive, and so do opinions.
development: A handful of words, points to ask for things, and scribbles.
feeding: Picky eating starts. Keep offering rejected foods without any pressure.
sleep: The two-nap to one-nap transition usually lands here.
heads_up: Fifteen-month check-up. Tantrums are a communication gap, not defiance.
facts: Tantrums start here. They are a language gap, not defiance, and they shorten as words arrive. | Picky eating is developmentally normal from about now. Keep offering the rejected food without comment.

label: 16–17 months
summary: Climbing everything.
development: Runs stiffly, climbs onto furniture, and follows one-step directions.
feeding: Three meals and two snacks on a predictable schedule beats grazing.
sleep: One afternoon nap of one to three hours.
heads_up: Anchor bookcases and televisions to the wall.
facts: Screens other than video calls are not recommended before 18–24 months. | Climbing starts in earnest: anchor bookcases and televisions to the wall.

label: 18–19 months
summary: Language takes off.
development: Often 10–25 words, points to body parts, and starts to play pretend.
feeding: Family meals at the same table — the same food cut smaller.
sleep: One nap. Bedtime resistance is common.
heads_up: The 18-month check-up includes an autism screening. Raise any speech concerns there.
facts: The 18-month visit includes autism screening as well as a general developmental check. | A vocabulary spurt is typical now. Fewer than ten words at 18 months is worth raising at that visit. | Naming what they point at, rather than just handing it over, is what turns pointing into words.

label: 20–21 months
summary: Doing it self.
development: Two-word phrases start and so does insisting on doing things alone.
feeding: Let {them} use a spoon and an open cup, badly, every day.
sleep: About 11–14 hours including the nap.
heads_up: Consistency beats reasoning at this age — short, calm, repeated limits.
facts: Letting them try it slowly and badly is the whole point — self-feeding and dressing attempts build the skill. | Two-word phrases usually start around now.

label: 22–23 months
summary: Approaching two.
development: Two-word sentences, kicks a ball, and copies absolutely everything you do.
feeding: Whole milk around 16 oz a day with water at meals.
sleep: Some start climbing out of the crib. A floor bed is worth considering.
heads_up: The two-year check-up plots BMI for the first time. Potty interest may begin and there is no rush.
facts: The two-year visit repeats autism screening and takes a first blood pressure. | Two-word sentences by 24 months is the usual expectation; raise it at the visit if they have not arrived. | Toilet training readiness is about staying dry for stretches and telling you afterwards — not about the birthday.
